conventions.statement: Original decimal digit string has fixed length L≥2, with nonzero first digit a; length is not recalculated after rotating.
Rotated digit string retains its fixed width even if it begins with a zero.
Ten is congruent to minus one modulo11.

microtopics.title: Explaining a place-value invariant and its length-sensitive failure
microtopics.badge_reason: Learner must explain why a digit rotation's invariant depends on original length, then diagnose the distinct two-digit-prefix exception.
entry_assumptions: Decimal place value and powers of ten.
Fixed-width cyclic rotation with the original nonzero first digit.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Explain why changing original length changes a place-value sign and flips whether a rotation preserves divisibility; under two-digit rotation the odd-length exception is different.

teaching_path.action: Use the decimal identity 10 congruent to -1 modulo 11: each shift by one decimal place changes the residue sign.
teaching_path.output: Sign-change mechanism independent of a particular digit string.

teaching_path.action: Compare two-digit 10u+v with digit-swapped 10v+u as a neutral worked anchor.
teaching_path.why_valid: Modulo11, the respective remainders are v-u and u-v.
teaching_path.output: For two positions, swapping negates residue, including zero.

teaching_path.action: Represent a general L-digit input with leading digit a and remaining value B as N=a×10^(L−1)+B; its one-digit left rotation is R=10B+a.
teaching_path.why_valid: Shifting the suffix left multiplies by ten and appending a adds its units value.
teaching_path.output: Exact positional equations, not the final parity classification.

teaching_path.action: Identify the assumption that must be rechecked whenever a two-digit demonstration is generalized to another original length.
teaching_path.why_valid: The contribution of a is multiplied by ten L−1 times; changing L changes that exponent.
teaching_path.output: Audit length and leading zero conventions before deciding the invariant.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Rotating a multiple of11 preserves divisibility for every digit length because it works for 22 and 1210.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Why does 121 rotate to 211, but 1210 rotates to 2101? Are these outcomes explained by the unchanged digit sum?
misconceptions.repair: Use the positions of digits modulo11. N=a10^(L−1)+B and R=10B+a; exponent parity, not digit sum, controls sign changes.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If rotation creates an initial zero, the original digit length changes and so should the rule.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Does 110 rotating two digits to 011 make the original three-digit statement into a two-digit one?
misconceptions.repair: Keep the original fixed-width L positions throughout each rotation; a new leading zero changes value but not the definition of the input operation.

exit_task.prompt: For any three-digit integer 100a+10b+c (a from1..9, b,c from0..9), explain why 11 divides it exactly when the alternating digit sum a-b+c is 0 OR 11, not just 0. Check 209.

answer.summary: The alternating sum can equal 0 or11.
reasoning: The allowed digit bounds make −8≤a−b+c≤18. The only multiples of11 in this interval are 0 and 11.
answer.check: 121 has sum0; 209 has sum11; both are divisible by11.

predict.prompt: A classmate says two-digit and four-digit rotations show every multiple of11 survives rotation at any length. Why could this rule fail for three-digit 121?
predict.defensible_answer: 121 rotates to211 and 211 is not divisible by11; tested even-digit cases do not establish all lengths.

rubric.evidence_of: Keeps domain correct under leading zeros.

rubric.criterion: Explain 10≡−1 modulo11 and its dependence on an exponent.
rubric.evidence_of: Causal place-value mechanism rather than digit-sum claim.

rubric.criterion: Explain why even L preserves zero residue and odd L yields nonzero 2a.
rubric.evidence_of: Correct causal effect of changed assumption.

rubric.criterion: Use odd-length boundary and a changed input to diagnose the overgeneralization.

accepted: For original N=a10^(L−1)+B with a nonzero first digit and rotation R=10B+a, modulo11 N≡a(-1)^(L−1)+B and R≡a−B. If L is even, R≡−N, so zero stays zero. If L is odd and N≡0, B≡−a, so R≡2a, nonzero because a is 1..9.
rejected: Digit sum stays constant so mod11 divisibility always stays constant.
The odd-length counterexample 121 is an arithmetic accident.

task.prompt: Explain why the assertion that ALL left one-digit rotations preserve 11-divisibility is wrong; use 121 and 1210 and the decimal place-value mechanism, not a table of many cases.
givens: Rotation keeps the original fixed width.

boundary_test.prompt: Predict whether left one-digit rotations of 110 and 1232 preserve divisibility by11, using original lengths. Then check 101 and 2321.
boundary_test.answer: 110 has odd original length and becomes101, not divisible by11; 1232 has even original length and becomes2321, divisible by11.
boundary_test.confirms: Repairs explanation on independent changed length and digits.

questions.stem: Verify q²−1=(q−1)(q+1). Explain how parity and modulo3 each affect the factorization, using q=3 as a conceptual boundary.
conditions: n is any integer, including negative integers and zero.

answer.summary: The two modular conditions are distinct.
reasoning: For odd q, two even neighbors spaced by2 supply factor8.
For q≡0 mod3 the expression is 2 mod3, while otherwise one neighbor supplies3.

family_exposure.closure: The concept worked anchor is not an independent QRT proof.

questions.stem: For all integers n, prove the exact necessary-and-sufficient criterion for 24 to divide n²−1. State all allowed residue classes modulo6 and prove both directions, including exceptions and a negative boundary.
conditions: n is any integer, including negative integers and zero.

reasoning: Sufficiency: for odd n, two even neighbors differ by2, giving factor8; if 3∤n a neighbor supplies factor3; coprimality yields24.
Necessity: even n has odd n²−1; a multiple of3 gives n²−1≡2 modulo3. Either cannot be divisible by24.
Thus n is odd and not divisible by3: exactly residues1 or5 modulo6.

reasoning_route.action: State integer domain and the two proof directions.
reasoning_route.why_valid: An iff assertion needs necessity and sufficiency.

reasoning_route.action: Prove both condition families and both converses.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Odd n forces factor8, nonmultiples of3 force factor3; even n or multiples of3 give universal obstructions.

reasoning_route.action: Independently inspect modulo24 residues and negative/zero cases.
reasoning_route.why_valid: All residue classes of integers are exhausted.

answer.check: n=-1 yields0 (yes); n=0 yields -1 (no); n=3 yields8 (no); n=5 yields24 (yes). Enumerate residues modulo24.

scaffolds.text: State precisely what an iff claim requires of an arbitrary integer. Separate the two directions.
Can you factor n²−1 into two neighbors? What kinds of prime-power factors would matter?
After recording your first attempt, audit factor8 and factor3 separately and use the excluded families to check necessity.

family_exposure.closure: No independent credit without both quantified proof directions.

difficulty.basis: Two-way universal iff with non-obvious exceptional families.

questions.stem: The divisor changes to 48. Prove exactly which residue classes modulo24 give 48|(n²−1) for arbitrary integers n. Show why the earlier 24-rule fails on a permitted input.
conditions: n is any integer, including negative integers and zero.

reasoning: For odd n modulo8, residues1,3,5,7 square modulo16 to1,9,9,1. Even n cannot work. Thus 16 divides exactly when n mod8 is1 or7.
3 divides the expression exactly when n is not divisible by3. Combining the two restrictions gives n mod24 in {1,7,17,23}.
n=5 gives n²−1=24, invalidating naive reuse of the earlier rule.

reasoning_route.action: Classify when 16 divides n²−1 via odd residues mod8.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The four odd classes square modulo16 to1,9,9,1.

reasoning_route.action: Combine factor16 and factor3 and list modulo24 classes.
reasoning_route.why_valid: gcd(16,3)=1 and mod24 encodes both residue conditions.

reasoning_route.action: Exhaust all modulo24 classes and falsify old rule using n=5.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Every integer has one class, and n=5 is admissible.

answer.check: Check classes1,7,17,23 modulo24 and n=5 as old-rule false positive.

rubric.criterion: Combine with mod3 to get four mod24 classes.

hints.text: Compare prime powers of 24 and48. Which extra factor2 is required?

difficulty.basis: A stronger power-of-two requirement changes the valid residue families.
